title: Why Trend Following Is Harder Than It Looks - Systematic Investor - Ep.405

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Why Trend Following Is Harder Than It Looks - Systematic Investor - Ep.405.docx

summary: Top Traders Unplugged Systematic Investor ep. 405 (June 2026): trend following conditions, why drawdown is a poor evaluation metric, perpetual futures, the Quantica paper on chasing sector trends (no value added), AI-assisted backtests and overfitting, and the Man paper on drawdowns.

coverage.note: Intro; peace deal and SpaceX index inclusion
New Fed chair Warsh, statistical data quality
Third-party data nowcasts; football banter; trend barometer 36; Rob positioning
Oil, metals, equities June moves; CTA index returns; listener question on Sharpe vs path risk
Drawdown as statistic; structural breaks; skew for classification
Skew caution; Factor Zoo paper
Beyond Passive Investing post: equity beta in trend following
Trend sleeve neutrality debate; CFTC perpetual futures intro
Perpetual futures vs variation margin mechanics
Perpetual futures as daily futures; pricing
Why perpetuals; CME lawsuit; hedgers
Futures market impact; Quantica paper: timing after drawdowns
Quantica sector rotation by decade
Single-factor explanation, continuous signals, null results
2010s as exception; commodity role in crises
1970s commodities; AI backtesting overfitting
Backtest process, probability weights
AI due diligence questions; Man Don't Look Down intro
Man drawdown paper
Outro and disclaimers - nothing actionable

completeness_estimate: 0.82 - the first reader caught the main arguments (drawdown vs Sharpe, skew buckets, trend sleeve neutrality, perpetual futures mechanics, Quantica findings, AI overfitting, Man drawdown paper) but missed the June performance table, the CTA convergent-strategy mix, the small-allocation rebuttal, the cocoa and AUM-incentive points, and the due-diligence process answer.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: in the olden days, you you couldn't get into an index unless you were profitable and they made adjustments for things like the free float of your shares.
claims.claim: Index providers are relaxing eligibility rules (profitability, free float) to admit SpaceX, which changes what index-based benchmarks and CTA indices represent.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the tone was a lot more hawkish uh than what he uh has been um uh
claims.claim: The new Fed chair Warsh was more hawkish than expected at his first FOMC, wants less forward guidance and a smaller balance sheet, and with high inflation there is little appetite for cuts.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we do have strategies in our world um that has come more recently that are economic trend or we have systematic global macro. Now, they do rely on this kind of data
claims.claim: Reworking or removing government survey data would hurt economic-trend and systematic global macro strategies that use economic releases, while pure price-based trend followers are unaffected.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: already been quite a serious
claims.claim: US statistical data quality has degraded (cuts, secrecy, delayed releases from the government shutdown), which weakens economic indicators used as forecasting inputs.
claims.testable: partly - data revisions and delays measurable

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there are third-party services that collect data and kind of forecast what the government statistics will be
claims.claim: Third-party nowcasting services can replace official statistics only if raw data remains available; deliberately removing data is dangerous for models trading on it.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: My trend barometer finished at 36 yesterday.
claims.claim: A trend barometer of 36 signals weak trend following conditions in June (weak equities, metals, grains; gains in short rates and the dollar).

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: The the biggest risk I have actually is in equities. I've got
claims.claim: A trend follower running only 9% annualized risk was positioned long equities (pro-deal) and flat energies, i.e. the portfolio mostly reflects the market's recent priced-in optimism.

correction.issue: The interpretation that the portfolio 'mostly reflects the market's recent priced-in optimism' is not stated. Rob describes his own book: 9% annualised risk (low), biggest risk a long equity position which he labels 'pro deal', and flat energies; the priced-in remark is a separate comment about the peace deal.
correction.fix: Rob Carver's own trend portfolio was running a low 9% annualised risk, with its largest risk a long equity position (pro peace deal) and no position in energies, so he was not positioned for the oil move.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: maybe this is one of those classic cases of, you know, buy the rumor, sell the sell the fact.
claims.claim: A peace deal that markets had priced in for weeks may produce buy the rumor, sell the fact, while oil supply shortages could keep normalization slow.
claims.indicator: oil complex around Hormuz peace deal

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the big market move so far in June has really been in the oil complex where we've seen kind of 15% drops in price.
claims.claim: In June 2026 oil fell about 15%, silver and platinum about 9%, offset by equities, shaping CTA returns (SocGen CTA about -0.8% in June, +9.5% YTD).
claims.indicator: oil, silver, platinum June moves; SocGen CTA index

correction.issue: 'offset by equities' misstates the market picture. The only equity gain cited is +7% for the Nifty (Indian equity future, which is Rob's biggest long); broad equities were down in June (S&P 500 -2%, MSCI World -1%), and the host earlier called equities weak.
correction.fix: In June 2026 oil fell about 15%, silver and platinum about 9% each, and these losses were partly offset only by a 7% gain in the Nifty future; broad equity indices were slightly down (S&P -2%, MSCI World -1%); SocGen CTA was about -0.8% in June and about +9.5% YTD.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the answer is, to be honest, um I tend
claims.claim: Sharpe ratio is the main metric for adding, sizing or removing a strategy; drop one only on very strong statistical evidence of a structural break.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: your drawdown's going to scale with the performance of your strategy and how long you've been running it for.
claims.claim: Drawdown is a poor evaluation statistic: ignoring autocorrelation it grows with history length and falls with Sharpe, so it adds no information beyond Sharpe.
claims.testable: yes - simulate drawdown vs Sharpe and length

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: potentially even going down the route of overfitting as well.
claims.claim: Looking at path risk and loss clustering for each individual strategy component overcomplicates and risks overfitting; it can matter at the whole-portfolio level.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I think that the issue becomes more when you're combining trend following with other things like carry
claims.claim: Skew is useful for classifying strategies into trend-like (positive skew) and carry-like (negative skew) buckets, because e.g. emerging-market FX carry has negative skew while developed bond carry is mildly positive.
claims.direction: limit negative-skew strategies to e.g. 30% of portfolio

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I'm wary of using skew in of itself as in sort of very constantative ways
claims.claim: Skew estimates are statistically unreliable, so use skew only as a classification device with a cap on the negative-skew bucket, not as a formal utility with Sharpe.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the more that these sort of the the fewer kind of real things that are driving the world the less help diversification's going to be for you.
claims.claim: The factor zoo has hundreds of factors but only a handful of independent drivers, so true diversification is less than the number of factors suggests.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you say trend follow equities, you will be on average net long equities.
claims.claim: Trend following in equities is on average net long, so part of its return is the equity risk premium plus extra return from sometimes being short.
claims.indicator: average equity beta of trend following

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if your trend following portfolio is say 20% of a bigger portfolio and that bigger portfolio is say 60/40
claims.claim: If trend following is a sleeve of a 60/40 portfolio, make it more neutral (long only when trend is strong) to avoid double-counting equity and bond premia.
claims.direction: reduce average equity and bond exposure in trend sleeve
claims.conditions: only if the sleeve is a small part of a portfolio already holding the premia

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think if you feel you have too much equity, you sell the equity. You let the trend following program run
claims.claim: Do not distort a trend program to fit the rest of the portfolio; adjust the other holdings, because distorting sectors changes the interaction among all markets.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it adds the market you don't trade yourself.
claims.claim: Trend following adds access to markets investors cannot easily trade themselves and is unbiased about long or short, e.g. fully short equities in a prolonged crisis.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: tilting your sector allocation within your CTA away from financials that most people already have exposure to and towards things like commodities
claims.claim: Within a CTA sleeve, tilt sector allocation away from financials (already held) toward commodities for better portfolio diversification.
claims.conditions: limited allocation to the CTA sleeve

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's basically a futures contract that, unlike every futures contract so far that has an expiration date, has no expiration date.
claims.claim: The CFTC approved the first perpetual futures contract (crypto), which is effectively a daily-settled future with no expiry.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: although these are called perpetual futures, what they really are in the sense is daily futures.
claims.claim: Perpetual futures are daily-settled futures whose cash flows equal variation margin, so futures price tracks spot (interest, dividend and storage costs are negligible) and no rolling is needed.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you're day trading it's a lot it's cheaper to to do it with a bet that closes today
claims.claim: Daily-settled instruments are cheaper for day traders since they avoid overnight funding costs, while exchange trading means only bid-ask costs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: clearly that has some massive implications for firms involved in the futures industry that rely on on volume
claims.claim: Perpetual futures would cut volume (no rolls) for exchanges; CME sued the CFTC arguing they are swaps, and hedgers like farmers need dated futures for price discovery.

correction.issue: Two speakers are merged. The volume loss for exchanges and the CME lawsuit against the CFTC (swap classification) are the host's; the points that futures began as hedging tools, that farmers need dated futures, and that price discovery needs a venue for hedgers are Rob Carver's.
correction.fix: Niels: perpetual futures would cut exchange volume (no rolls) and the CME sued the CFTC over approval, arguing they are swaps. Rob (separate point): futures began as hedging instruments, so farmers need dated futures, and price discovery needs a venue where producers and consumers hedge even though most volume is speculative.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I think sort of for the futures market generally, I'm not sure it's a a great development, to be honest.
claims.claim: If perpetuals shift hedging to OTC swaps liquidity and spreads worsen as capacity is split, and trading may concentrate in market-maker houses.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: So, I've done research and other people have done research on, for example, whether you should get out of trend following or get into trend following after drawdowns.
claims.claim: Timing entry or exit of trend following by recent drawdowns does not work: return autocorrelation is too weak to predict returns after drawdowns.
claims.indicator: autocorrelation of trend following returns after drawdowns

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you are paying performance fees, then you absolutely want to invest in a in a fund when it's in a drawdown
claims.claim: An investor in a fund below its high-water mark gets the first returns without performance fees, unless in a separate share class with its own high-water mark.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if we look at the performance of trend following in different asset classes over time, we see some very interesting patterns.
claims.claim: Quantica: trend following P&L by sector rotates across decades: 2000-09 split equities/currencies/commodities, 2010-19 almost all fixed income, 2020-26 mostly commodities with equities detracting.
claims.indicator: trend following P&L by asset class by decade

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: in these periods when one asset class is dominating, it's very much about a a sort of single factor that's driving everything.
claims.claim: Dominance of one asset class in trend returns is a single-factor story (e.g. predictable rate cuts and hikes), not diversification, so shifting into the hot sector reduces diversification.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: by allocating to things with stronger trends, which is what you do naturally if you've got a continuous system, that allocation is already happening.
claims.claim: A continuous (trend-strength scaled) signal already tilts toward asset classes with stronger trends, so extra performance chasing of asset classes is unnecessary and does not add return.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: It's just as valuable to find out that something isn't working as to find out that something is working.
claims.claim: Publishing null results is a sign of good research; Quantica found tactical asset-class chasing does not add value.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: that decade was not the new norm it's the odd one out.
claims.claim: The 2010-19 fixed-income-driven trend period, with zero rates and central banks suppressing inflation, was the exception; earlier decades and the 2020s show more diverse contribution including commodities.

correction.issue: Stated as observed fact, but it is the host's conjecture. The Quantica paper covers only 2000-2026; Niels says he would have liked the 1990s and 1980s included and thinks they would look more like 2000-09 or the 2020s.
correction.fix: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen: the 2010-19 fixed-income-driven decade (zero rates, central banks suppressing inflation) was the odd one out, not the new norm; he expects (not shown in the paper) that the 1970s-90s looked more like 2000-09 and 2020-26 with commodities contributing strongly.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the most consistent sector in a crisis is the commodity sector
claims.claim: A reputable study found commodities are the most consistent trend sector in crises, so a portfolio should include many truly uncorrelated markets rather than overweight liquid financial markets.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the inflation of the 1970s was fantastic for commodities trend following.
claims.claim: The 1970s inflation was excellent for commodity trend following.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's fine to use AI essentially to generate ideas, to generate strategy ideas.
claims.claim: AI is fine for idea generation but ideas must be tested in a robust process away from the AI, because the process matters more than the maths.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: that idea will almost certainly have been conceptualized using future information that you wouldn't have had at the start of your back test.
claims.claim: Any idea, from AI or data mining, is conceived with hindsight, so a backtest process must handle look-ahead contamination robustly.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: It's going to be a a probability that it's good and that will translate then into a portfolio weight.
claims.claim: The output of backtesting should be a probability that a strategy works translating into a portfolio weight (outstanding idea 10-15%, weak idea about 0.01%), not a yes/no decision.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: did you train it on, say, data before a certain date and then have a pure out-of-sample period?
claims.claim: Due diligence on AI-driven strategies should ask whether models are internal or external and whether trained before a date with a pure out-of-sample test; public AI models may contain forward information.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: he does actually define drawdowns, which is which is quite useful.
claims.claim: Drawdown studies need a definition because strictly one is in drawdown almost always; across 50 years there are only 10-20 episodes, so conclusions across assets are statistically weak.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: when these assets were in a drawdown what other assets tend to be in a drawdown or not in a drawdown.
claims.claim: Man paper: examine joint drawdown behaviour across assets as a more rigorous crisis-alpha test than cherry-picked stress periods (e.g. omitting COVID, when trend followers did less well).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the Beta 50 index as of Tuesday is down 85 basis points for the month, up 8.76% so far this this year
claims.claim: Mid-June 2026 performance data: BTOP50 -85bp in June (+8.76% YTD), SG CTA -81bp (about +9.5% YTD), SG Trend about -1.25% (+9% YTD), short-term traders -0.25% (+5% YTD), versus MSCI World about -1% (+9% YTD), US Aggregate bonds flat (+0.5% YTD) and S&P 500 -2% (+9% YTD), so CTA indices roughly matched equities year to date with a small June loss.
claims.indicator: BTOP50; SG CTA Index; SG Trend Index; SG Short-Term Traders Index; MSCI World; US Aggregate; S&P 500

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: they'll have, you know, a 20 or a 30% allocation to what you might call divergent strategies.
claims.claim: Almost no CTA is a pure trend follower: they typically hold 20-30% in convergent (non-trend, e.g. carry) strategies, while Rob Carver holds 40% because he has no client pool or allocator box to fit, so the trend/non-trend mix is a design choice constrained by clients.
claims.indicator: share of non-trend strategies in a CTA program
claims.conditions: the speaker misspeaks 'divergent' and corrects himself to 'convergent'
claims.testable: partly - mix of trend and carry can be backtested

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: momentum, which is different from a trend following cuz it's a relative factor, not an absolute factor
claims.claim: Cross-sectional momentum is a relative factor (winners against losers) whereas trend following is an absolute, time-series factor, so the two should not be treated as the same source of return when counting factors.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you'll get a better portfolio overall if that five or 10 or 15 or 20% has less exposure overall to equities and bonds than than otherwise
claims.claim: Rebuttal to the host: investors who can only allocate 5-20% to a CTA sleeve (not restructure their 60/40) get a better total portfolio if the sleeve carries less equity and bond beta; the ideal is a bigger CTA bucket, but that is often not an option. Niels counters that with only 5% in trend the sleeve's equity exposure is not worth worrying about.
claims.indicator: equity and bond beta of the trend sleeve
claims.direction: reduce average equity/bond exposure inside a small trend sleeve
claims.conditions: small CTA allocation inside a 60/40 portfolio; disputed by the host
claims.testable: yes - backtest neutralised vs standard trend sleeve in a 60/40

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Let's leave cocoa out because it didn't perform for 15 years and bang, you missed the the biggest trend it's ever had.
claims.claim: Dropping markets that have not trended recently is dangerous: cocoa was idle for 15 years and then produced its biggest trend ever, so rotating only into the best recent performers would have missed it.
claims.direction: keep all markets in the universe
claims.testable: yes - compare full universe with performance-chasing allocation

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: First of all, is there a reason why this is happening? Are there are there different explanations for why this is happening? And secondly, can I exploit this apparent predictability in some way?
claims.claim: Faced with a pattern such as sector leadership rotating by decade, a quant should first ask why it happens and whether other explanations fit, and only then ask whether it can be exploited (e.g. shifting weight to the hot asset class).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you go back 20, 25 years, I mean, even through this bull market of equities
claims.claim: Over 20-25 years, even through the long equity bull market, equities have not been a strong contributor to trend following P&L, so the financial-sector bias of many CTAs has not been rewarded by equities.
claims.indicator: equity sector share of trend P&L
claims.conditions: uses data the speaker had access to, not shown
claims.testable: yes - sector attribution of a trend index

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: focus more and more of the portfolio towards financial markets because they're more liquid usually and therefore you can manage more money
claims.claim: CTAs have drifted toward liquid financial markets because capacity lets them run more assets and managers are paid on assets managed, an incentive that works against the more diversified commodity-heavy portfolio the speaker favours.
claims.testable: partly - sector weights of CTA indices

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I've never used it to write any you know more than about 10 lines of code cuz I just don't trust it enough and I spend more time checking and rewriting it.
claims.claim: AI-written code and AI-run backtests cost more in checking and rewriting than they save, so AI is used for ideas and small snippets and never trusted to run a strategy backtest.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: tell me what happens from through that process, from idea to live trading. What are the steps in that process? What are the checks and balances?
claims.claim: Due diligence on a CTA should focus on the research process from idea to live trading (steps, checks and balances, robustness, peer review), which is the same whether the idea came from an AI, a junior researcher or data mining, because every idea is formed with forward information and the AI's own evaluation of itself should not be trusted.
claims.conditions: AI-specific questions only needed when the process is flawed
